questions.q: What problem does API versioning solve, per this lesson?
options: It lets a provider's API contract evolve over time without breaking every existing caller still depending on the version they originally built against
It eliminates the need for any interface documentation
It guarantees an API will never need to change its behavior
It is only relevant for the Bulk API, not for REST or SOAP
questions.explain: Versioning lets multiple versions of an API coexist, each caller specifying which one it uses, so a contract can evolve for new callers without breaking existing callers who haven't updated yet.

questions.q: Adding a new, optional field to an API response that existing callers simply ignore is an example of what kind of change?
options: A breaking change requiring an immediate new version
A backward-compatible change, since existing callers aren't affected by a field they don't know about and don't need
An undefined change with no classification
A deprecation event
questions.explain: A backward-compatible change, like an optional new field, doesn't break any existing caller — the caller simply ignores the new field — so it generally doesn't require a new API version.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a breaking change, per this lesson's definition?
options: Adding a new optional request parameter
Adding a new optional response field
Renaming a field an existing caller depends on
Adding documentation for an existing field
questions.explain: Renaming a field breaks any existing caller that depends on the original field name — exactly the category of change that justifies, and requires, a new API version rather than silently altering the version already in use.

questions.q: How does Salesforce's REST API versioning work conceptually, and what does pinning an integration to an older version mean architecturally?
options: Salesforce only ever supports one API version at a time, and all integrations must update immediately on every release

Salesforce versions its REST API numerically alongside each major release and maintains multiple versions concurrently; an integration pinned to an older version doesn't automatically get new capabilities and has to explicitly update its version string to receive them
API versioning does not apply to Salesforce's own REST API, only to third-party APIs
Pinning to an older API version is always a sign of a misconfigured integration with no legitimate use
questions.explain: Salesforce releases a new numbered API version alongside each major release and supports multiple versions concurrently; an integration pinned to an older version keeps working but must explicitly bump its version string to pick up newer capabilities or to pick up a changed behavior introduced in a later version.

questions.q: What failure mode does a published deprecation policy with a sunset date exist to prevent?
options: A provider silently removing an old API version with no warning, breaking every caller still on it overnight with no time to react
Callers using too many different API versions simultaneously
An API provider releasing too many new features too quickly
Integrations being built using an outdated programming language
questions.explain: A deprecation policy gives callers advance notice of when a version will stop being supported, specifically preventing the scenario where a provider removes support with no warning and breaks every caller still depending on that version overnight.
